text: This is it — the capstone, and the final chapter of this course. The next three lessons pull together the Black-Scholes model and the Greeks from Chapter 3, and the hedging ideas from Chapter 5, into one connected project: build a small options portfolio, price it, measure its risk, and hedge it. This lesson sets up the project. The next one does the actual math and code.

Here's the setup. We're using a fictional stock, ZQX Inc, trading at a hundred dollars, with a three percent risk-free rate throughout. The portfolio holds three options: option A is an at-the-money call, strike one hundred, six months out, twenty-five percent implied vol, ten contracts long. Option B is an out-of-the-money call, strike one-ten, three months out, thirty percent vol, five contracts long. And option C is an out-of-the-money put, strike ninety-five, six months out, twenty-five percent vol — but this one is short, eight contracts written rather than bought. Every contract covers a hundred shares, the standard convention.

Four concrete deliverables come out of the next lesson. First, a Black-Scholes price for each of the three options. Second, delta, gamma, and vega for each one individually. Third, those Greeks aggregated up to the portfolio level, with the short put position contributing with a flipped sign. And fourth, the actual hedge trade: how many shares of ZQX to buy or sell so the portfolio's net delta comes out to zero.

Why target delta specifically? Delta measures directional exposure, and it's usually the largest single risk sitting in an options book. A share of the underlying has a delta of exactly one, which is what makes it possible to offset a portfolio's delta directly with a stock position — buy or sell exactly enough shares and the net delta goes to zero. That said, flattening delta isn't the same as making the portfolio risk-free. Gamma and vega exposure remain even after delta is flat, and that's exactly where Lesson 33 picks the story back up.

The setup is in place: ZQX Inc at a hundred dollars, three options with different strikes and maturities, a mix of long and short positions, and a clear goal — price it, measure it, flatten its delta. Up next, Lesson 32: Capstone, Build It, where these numbers actually get run through the math.
